questions.question: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed in 1848 between the United States and:
questions.correctAnswer: Mexico
distractors: Spain
France
Texas as an independent nation
questions.explanation: Signed February 2, 1848 outside Mexico City, the treaty ended the Mexican-American War. Mexico ceded roughly half its territory - including New Mexico and California - for $15 million and the assumption of claims.
questions.memoryHook: 1848: the United States and Mexico sign; the map is redrawn.

img.scene: A treaty table with two flags and a large map of North America spread between them. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 1848: the United States and Mexico sign; the map is redrawn.
img.title: THE TREATY OF 1848

questions.question: Article IX of the treaty promised Mexican citizens who remained in the ceded territories:
questions.correctAnswer: Enjoyment of their liberty, property and civil rights, with admission to United States citizenship
distractors: Immediate removal to Mexico at federal expense
Exemption from all taxes for one hundred years
A separate Mexican state inside the United States
questions.explanation: Article IX pledged that those who stayed would be 'maintained and protected in the free enjoyment of their liberty and property' and admitted to citizenship. Roughly nine of ten eligible people chose to stay and become citizens.
questions.memoryHook: Article IX: stay, keep your property, become citizens.

img.scene: Families standing before their adobe homes with fields and a church behind them, calm light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Article IX: stay, keep your property, become citizens.
img.title: ARTICLE IX PROMISES

questions.question: The United States Senate struck Article X from the treaty before ratification. Article X would have:
questions.correctAnswer: Expressly guaranteed the validity of Mexican and Spanish land grants in the ceded territory
distractors: Banned the Spanish language in New Mexico
Returned Texas to Mexico in ten years
Given Mexico control of the Rio Grande forever
questions.explanation: Article X stated that land grants 'shall be respected as valid.' Its deletion - softened only by the Protocol of Queretaro's assurances - forced every grant into case-by-case American confirmation, the root of a century of land loss.
questions.memoryHook: The struck Article X is the hinge of New Mexico land history.

img.scene: A document with one paragraph crossed out resting beside survey maps and a brass seal. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The struck Article X is the hinge of New Mexico land history.
img.title: THE STRICKEN ARTICLE X

questions.question: The Protocol of Queretaro (May 1848) was added to answer Mexican fears after Article X was struck. It stated that:
questions.correctAnswer: The United States did not intend by the deletion to annul legitimate Mexican land grants
distractors: All grants were cancelled but would be repaid in gold
New Mexico would be returned if grants were disputed
Grant holders must convert to Protestantism
questions.explanation: American negotiators assured Mexico the deletion changed nothing in principle: legitimate titles would still be respected. Grant heirs later cited the protocol in court - usually without success against procedural rulings and survey decisions.
questions.memoryHook: Queretaro promised the deletion changed nothing. Courts decided otherwise.

img.scene: Two officials exchanging a sealed protocol document across a table in a plain government room. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Queretaro promised the deletion changed nothing. Courts decided otherwise.
img.title: THE PROTOCOL OF QUERETARO

questions.question: Under the treaty, a Mexican citizen in Santa Fe in 1848 who did nothing at all within one year would:
questions.correctAnswer: Be treated as having elected United States citizenship
distractors: Lose all property automatically
Be deported to Mexico City
Become a citizen of Spain again
questions.explanation: Article VIII gave residents one year to declare Mexican citizenship and leave with their property; silence meant choosing the United States. Almost everyone stayed - homes, grants, graves and communities outweighed the uncertain south.
questions.memoryHook: Silence meant staying: nine in ten became Americans by default.

img.scene: A village plaza with families going about market day beneath a new flag on the palace. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Silence meant staying: nine in ten became Americans by default.
img.title: CHOOSING TO STAY

questions.question: Why did the treaty's property guarantees prove weaker in practice than on paper?
questions.correctAnswer: Confirmation required English-language proceedings, surveys and lawyers in distant forums, and communal grant lands were often ruled individual or public property
distractors: The treaty text was never translated into English
Congress repealed the treaty itself in 1850
Grant documents had all been destroyed in the war
questions.explanation: The Surveyor General and later the Court of Private Land Claims (1891) confirmed only a fraction of claimed acreage. Ejido commons were especially vulnerable: American law struggled to recognize land held by a whole community rather than a person.
questions.memoryHook: Paper rights met procedure; procedure won most rounds.

img.scene: Heirs studying a faded grant map by lamplight while legal ledgers stack beside it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Paper rights met procedure; procedure won most rounds.
img.title: PAPER VERSUS PROCEDURE

questions.question: The Court of Private Land Claims, created in 1891, decided New Mexico grant cases and ultimately:
questions.correctAnswer: Confirmed only a small share - roughly 6 percent - of the acreage claimed before it
distractors: Confirmed every grant exactly as claimed
Returned all disputed land to Mexico
Abolished private land ownership in New Mexico
questions.explanation: Of some 35 million acres claimed in New Mexico cases, the court confirmed about 2 million. Rejected commons often passed to the public domain - today's national forests include former grant lands, a grievance still alive in northern villages.
questions.memoryHook: Six percent confirmed: the Court of Private Land Claims in one figure.

img.scene: A courtroom bench with thick claim files, a survey map pinned behind it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Six percent confirmed: the Court of Private Land Claims in one figure.
img.title: THE LAND CLAIMS COURT

questions.question: The Maxwell Land Grant became the largest confirmed grant in United States history and symbolized the era because:
questions.correctAnswer: Some 1.7 million acres passed from community origins through Beaubien and Miranda heirs to Anglo investors and a Dutch company
distractors: It was returned intact to its original villages in 1900
It covered the entire state of New Mexico
It was never claimed by anyone after 1848
questions.explanation: Confirmed at about 1.7 million acres, the Maxwell grant was sold to investors, fenced against settlers and grant heirs, and defended in the Colfax County War. It is the textbook case of treaty property converted into corporate property.
questions.memoryHook: Maxwell: 1.7 million acres from village grant to corporation.

img.scene: Barbed wire fencing stretching across a vast valley toward a mountain peak, old farmsteads beyond. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Maxwell: 1.7 million acres from village grant to corporation.
img.title: THE MAXWELL GRANT

questions.question: A historian arguing that the treaty era 'never ended' for New Mexico would point most strongly to:
questions.correctAnswer: Continuing land-grant heir organizations, water-rights adjudications and treaty-rights claims in modern courts and politics
distractors: The survival of the Mexican army in New Mexico
New Mexico's refusal to join the Union in 1912
A ban on English in the state constitution
questions.explanation: The Aamodt and Abeyta water adjudications, grant-heir mercedes, and GAO reports of 2001 and 2004 all descend from 1848's promises. Treaty history in New Mexico is not past tense - it is docketed.
questions.memoryHook: 1848 is still on the docket.

img.scene: A modern courthouse steps scene with elders carrying an old framed grant document. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 1848 is still on the docket.
img.title: STILL ON THE DOCKET

questions.question: The Gadsden Purchase (1853-54) completed the present New Mexico boundary by adding:
questions.correctAnswer: The southern strip including Mesilla, bought from Mexico for a southern railroad route
distractors: The Four Corners region from Utah Territory
The Texas Panhandle from the Republic of Texas
The Gila headwaters from Spain
questions.explanation: For $10 million the United States bought the flat corridor south of the Gila River. Mesilla briefly became a Confederate Arizona capital in 1861-62, then settled into New Mexico - its valley still farms the Rio Grande's water.
questions.memoryHook: Gadsden's strip finished the map in 1854.

img.scene: A railroad survey crew on a flat valley floor with a river, fields and a border monument nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Gadsden's strip finished the map in 1854.
img.title: FINISHING THE MAP

questions.question: New Mexico remained a territory from 1850 until statehood in:
questions.explanation: Admitted January 6, 1912 as the 47th state, New Mexico waited 62 years - among the longest territorial apprenticeships in American history. Arizona followed six weeks later as the 48th.
questions.memoryHook: 1912: the 47th state, after 62 territorial years.

img.scene: A star being sewn onto a flag in a capitol workshop, bunting and ladders nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 1912: the 47th state, after 62 territorial years.
img.title: STATEHOOD IN 1912

questions.question: Railroads reached New Mexico in 1878-1880 and most directly transformed the territory by:
questions.correctAnswer: Connecting mines, ranches and farms to national markets and founding new depot towns
distractors: Ending all wagon and stage travel in a single day
Making Santa Fe a Pacific seaport
Replacing Spanish with English in one year by law
questions.explanation: The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe crossed Raton Pass in 1878; Las Vegas, Albuquerque New Town and Deming rose as rail towns. Coal from Raton, cattle from the plains and copper from the south now moved by the carload.
questions.memoryHook: Rails after 1878 rewired the territory's economy.

img.scene: A steam train crossing a high desert trestle toward a new depot town at sunset. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Rails after 1878 rewired the territory's economy.
img.title: RAILS REWIRE THE TERRITORY

questions.question: The Civil War in New Mexico was decided less by the fighting in Glorieta Pass itself than by:
questions.correctAnswer: The destruction of the Confederate supply train, which forced Sibley's invasion to retreat to Texas
distractors: A naval blockade of the Rio Grande
The capture of Richmond by New Mexico troops
A treaty signed in Santa Fe in 1862
questions.explanation: Chivington's flank march - guided by Manuel Chavez - burned about 80 wagons at Johnson's Ranch. The battles of Valverde and Glorieta mattered, but an army without food in a desert it had stripped could only go home.
questions.memoryHook: No supplies, no invasion: Glorieta's supply train was the campaign.

img.scene: Charred wagon remains in a mountain valley clearing, pines and cliffs around it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: No supplies, no invasion: Glorieta's supply train was the campaign.
img.title: SUPPLY TRAIN DESTROYED

questions.question: Boarding schools such as the Albuquerque Indian School (founded 1881) were built on the federal policy of:
questions.correctAnswer: Forced assimilation - removing Native children from families to erase languages and cultures
distractors: Bilingual education designed by tribal governments
Voluntary exchange programs run by the Pueblos
Teaching only college-level science to adults
questions.explanation: Under 'kill the Indian, save the man' logic, children were punished for speaking their languages, given English names and trained for manual labor. Survivors' accounts and the 2022 federal boarding-school report document deaths, abuse and cultural loss - and Native resilience in response.
questions.memoryHook: Boarding schools aimed at assimilation; children paid the price.

img.scene: An empty school dormitory corridor with rows of narrow beds, cold window light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Boarding schools aimed at assimilation; children paid the price.
img.title: THE BOARDING SCHOOLS

questions.question: The Homestead Act affected New Mexico differently from the humid Midwest because:
questions.correctAnswer: 160 dry acres often could not support a family, so ranching claims were combined, fenced or fraudulently assembled into large spreads
distractors: Homesteaders were banned from New Mexico by law
Every New Mexico claim succeeded within one year
The Act applied only east of the Mississippi
questions.explanation: Congress eventually enlarged dry-land homesteads (320 acres in 1909, 640 for stock-raising in 1916), conceding the original quarter-section was a humid-land measure. In New Mexico, water - not acreage - was the true limit on a claim.
questions.memoryHook: In dry country, 160 acres is a garden, not a ranch.

img.scene: A lone homestead cabin on a vast dry plain, a windmill and a small fenced plot beside it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: In dry country, 160 acres is a garden, not a ranch.
img.title: HOMESTEADING THE DRY LAND

questions.question: New Mexico's statehood was repeatedly blocked in Congress by objections that historians summarize as:
questions.correctAnswer: Prejudice against its Spanish-speaking Catholic majority, plus partisan calculation and land-grant and language anxieties
distractors: New Mexico's complete lack of a constitution draft in any year
A territorial law banning American citizens from settling
The territory's refusal to hold any elections for 60 years
questions.explanation: Territorial delegates lobbied for decades; joint statehood with Arizona was proposed in 1906 and rejected by Arizona voters. Only in 1910 did Congress pass the Enabling Act letting New Mexico write its 1910-11 constitution.
questions.memoryHook: Language, faith and party math blocked the door until 1910.

img.scene: A delegate with a thick petition waiting outside a closed committee-room door in a marble hall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Language, faith and party math blocked the door until 1910.
img.title: BLOCKED AT THE DOOR

questions.question: The 1910-11 New Mexico constitutional convention deliberately wrote protections for Spanish-speaking citizens, including:
questions.correctAnswer: Safeguards for voting and education rights regardless of language, and a bar on segregating children of Spanish descent in public schools
distractors: A law making Spanish the only official language
A rule that all laws be printed only in Spanish
Exemption of Spanish speakers from taxation
questions.explanation: Article XII forbade segregating 'children of Spanish descent' and required bilingual teacher training; Article VII protected the franchise. So central were these clauses that amending parts of the constitution requires extraordinary majorities - a shield built in 1911.
questions.memoryHook: The 1911 constitution locked Spanish-speakers' rights in a hard-to-amend vault.

img.scene: Delegates at a long table drafting a document, two flags and a bust in the hall behind them. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The 1911 constitution locked Spanish-speakers' rights in a hard-to-amend vault.
img.title: RIGHTS WRITTEN IN, 1911

questions.question: Land redistribution pressures in the territorial era produced Las Gorras Blancas (the White Caps), who:
questions.correctAnswer: Cut fences and campaigned in San Miguel County (1889-1891) against the enclosure of community grant commons by speculators and railroads
distractors: Burned the territorial capitol to the ground
Founded the Republican Party in New Mexico
Patrolled the Mexican border for the army
questions.explanation: Night riders in white caps cut barbed wire that fenced Las Vegas grant commons; the movement flowed into El Partido del Pueblo Unido's electoral wins in 1890. Fencing - a technology and a legal theory - was the enemy they named.
questions.memoryHook: White Caps cut the wire that stole the commons.

img.scene: Cut strands of barbed wire fence on open rangeland under moonlight, gloves and tools on the ground. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: White Caps cut the wire that stole the commons.
img.title: LAS GORRAS BLANCAS

questions.question: Race and land in territorial New Mexico were linked most visibly in Colfax County, where:
questions.correctAnswer: The Maxwell grant's new owners fought settlers and grant heirs in the Colfax County War (1875-1878), with killings on both sides
distractors: A peace treaty gave the county jointly to two nations
Gold miners voted the county out of the territory
The railroad surrendered all its lands to villages
questions.explanation: When the Maxwell company tried to evict settlers and heirs, resistance led by figures like Clay Allison and the murdered Rev. F.J. Tolby turned violent. The war showed how treaty land transfers became gunfights on the ground.
questions.memoryHook: Colfax: where land paper turned to gunfire.

img.scene: A deserted county courthouse square at dusk, a toppled fence and an empty street. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Colfax: where land paper turned to gunfire.
img.title: THE COLFAX COUNTY WAR

questions.question: Territorial New Mexico's population and economy by 1900 are best described as:
questions.correctAnswer: Still majority Hispano and Native, ranching and mining based, with rail towns layering Anglo commerce onto older plaza communities
distractors: Entirely Anglo and industrial, with no Spanish spoken
Smaller than it had been in 1800 due to total abandonment
Dependent chiefly on Pacific shipping
questions.explanation: The 1900 census counted about 195,000 people. Old villages held their language and grants while mines at White Oaks, Silver City and Raton and the cattle boom pulled in Anglo capital - a layered society statehood would inherit.
questions.memoryHook: 1900: old villages below, rail commerce above - one layered society.

img.scene: An old adobe plaza and a brick rail-town main street sharing one valley view at golden hour. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 1900: old villages below, rail commerce above - one layered society.
img.title: A LAYERED SOCIETY, 1900

questions.question: New Mexico government has executive, legislative and judicial branches. Its legislature is distinctive because:
questions.correctAnswer: Citizen legislators serve without a salary - only per diem and mileage - in 30- or 60-day sessions
distractors: It meets every day of the year like Congress
Its members are appointed by the governor for life
It has only one chamber of nine members
questions.explanation: New Mexico's 70 House members and 42 senators are unpaid volunteers in the nation's last true citizen legislature. Short sessions - 60 days in odd years, 30 in even - make speed and interim committees central to lawmaking.
questions.memoryHook: Unpaid, part-time, citizen lawmakers: New Mexico's legislature.

img.scene: A round capitol building chamber with rows of wooden desks under a high ceiling. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Unpaid, part-time, citizen lawmakers: New Mexico's legislature.
img.title: THE CITIZEN LEGISLATURE

questions.question: The Roundhouse in Santa Fe is:
questions.correctAnswer: New Mexico's state capitol, built in 1966 in the shape of the Zia sun symbol
distractors: A Pueblo ceremonial structure from the 1400s
The territorial prison built in 1856
A railroad roundhouse still used for locomotives
questions.explanation: The capitol's circular plan echoes the Zia symbol that also centers the state flag - four rays in four directions. It is the country's only round statehouse, housing the legislature and governor's office.
questions.memoryHook: The Roundhouse: a capitol shaped like the Zia sun.

img.scene: A circular sandstone-colored capitol building with a central skylight dome under blue sky. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Roundhouse: a capitol shaped like the Zia sun.
img.title: THE ROUNDHOUSE

questions.question: Tribal sovereignty in New Mexico means the state's 23 federally recognized tribes:
questions.correctAnswer: Govern themselves as sovereign nations with their own constitutions, courts and police, in a government-to-government relationship with the state and the United States
distractors: Are departments administered by the state governor
Hold only ceremonial status with no legal authority
Must dissolve their governments under state law
questions.explanation: Nineteen Pueblos, two Apache tribes and the Navajo Nation (plus the Fort Sill Apache Tribe's New Mexico presence) exercise inherent sovereignty recognized by treaties and federal law. The 2009 State-Tribal Collaboration Act requires state agencies to consult tribal governments.
questions.memoryHook: Sovereign nations inside one state: that is New Mexico's structure.

img.scene: Tribal and state flags standing side by side in a row outside a government building. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Sovereign nations inside one state: that is New Mexico's structure.
img.title: SOVEREIGN NATIONS

questions.question: How do New Mexico's Pueblos typically govern themselves?
questions.correctAnswer: Through governors and councils rooted in traditional leadership, with officers such as governors often selected through theocratic or community processes and recognized with Spanish-era canes
distractors: By mayors elected under the state municipal code only
By direct administration from the Bureau of Indian Affairs
By hereditary kings confirmed by Congress
questions.explanation: Pueblo governments blend ancient theocratic structures with offices layered by Spain (governors, war captains) and the United States. Lincoln canes - presented in 1863-64 to pueblo governors - remain symbols of recognized authority.
questions.memoryHook: Canes, councils and custom: Pueblo government is layered and living.

img.scene: A row of engraved silver-headed canes resting on a blanket in soft window light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Canes, councils and custom: Pueblo government is layered and living.
img.title: CANES OF OFFICE

questions.question: The Navajo Nation's government, whose capital is Window Rock, Arizona, exercises jurisdiction in New Mexico mainly in:
questions.correctAnswer: The eastern portion of the Navajo Nation chapters - such as Ramah, Alamo and Tohajiilee communities and the eastern agency - within New Mexico's borders
distractors: The city government of Santa Fe
All counties of northern New Mexico
No part of New Mexico at all
questions.explanation: The Navajo Nation spans three states; its New Mexico chapters include both reservation communities and the Ramah, Alamo and Tohajiilee (Canoncito) bands. Chapter houses function as local government for citizens there.
questions.memoryHook: Window Rock governs chapters that reach deep into New Mexico.

img.scene: A chapter house building beneath red sandstone cliffs with a natural rock window arch beyond. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Window Rock governs chapters that reach deep into New Mexico.
img.title: WINDOW ROCK'S REACH

questions.question: When a state highway project may affect a New Mexico tribe's cultural sites, the State-Tribal Collaboration Act of 2009 requires state agencies to:
questions.correctAnswer: Consult with tribal governments on a government-to-government basis before acting
distractors: Proceed without notice if the project is federally funded
Ask county commissioners to decide for the tribe
Publish a newspaper notice and wait ten days
questions.explanation: The Act institutionalized consultation, tribal liaisons and an annual state-tribal leaders' summit. It recognizes that tribes are governments to be negotiated with - not interest groups to be informed afterward.
questions.memoryHook: Consult first: tribes are governments, not interest groups.

img.scene: State and tribal officials seated around a large round table with flags behind them. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Consult first: tribes are governments, not interest groups.
img.title: CONSULT FIRST

questions.question: New Mexico's judiciary differs from the federal system in that state judges:
questions.correctAnswer: Are elected by voters in partisan elections, then face nonpartisan retention elections
distractors: Are appointed for life by the governor alone
Are chosen by the tribal councils of each district
Serve without any elections at all
questions.explanation: After initial partisan election, New Mexico judges must win 57 percent in retention votes to keep their seats - a hybrid of election and appointment politics unusual among the states.
questions.memoryHook: Elected once by party, kept by 57 percent: New Mexico judges.

img.scene: A courtroom with a long bench, a state flag and wooden counsel tables in quiet light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Elected once by party, kept by 57 percent: New Mexico judges.
img.title: JUDGES AND RETENTION

questions.question: Counties and municipalities in New Mexico get their powers from:
questions.correctAnswer: The state constitution and statutes - counties as arms of the state, with home-rule charters available to qualifying municipalities and counties
distractors: The United States Constitution directly, listing each county by name
Tribal governments within their borders
Private charters sold by the legislature in 1850
questions.explanation: New Mexico follows Dillon's Rule for counties; Albuquerque and a few others hold home-rule charters granting broader self-government. Above both sit tribal and federal jurisdictions that neither county nor city law can displace.
questions.memoryHook: Counties serve the state; charters free the cities; tribes stand apart.

img.scene: A county courthouse, a city hall and a tribal government building along one valley road. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Counties serve the state; charters free the cities; tribes stand apart.
img.title: LAYERS OF GOVERNMENT

questions.question: Indian gaming in New Mexico operates under:
questions.correctAnswer: Compacts negotiated between the state and tribal governments under the federal Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, sharing revenue with the state
distractors: A state law banning all gaming on tribal land
County licenses issued like tavern permits
A treaty from 1848 that set casino rules
questions.explanation: The 2001 and later compacts let tribal casinos operate Class III gaming in exchange for revenue sharing and regulation. Gaming income funds tribal government services - a modern exercise of the sovereignty the compacts presuppose.
questions.memoryHook: Compacts, not county permits: gaming is sovereignty negotiated.

img.scene: A tribal resort building at dusk beneath desert mountains, lights coming on along its facade. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Compacts, not county permits: gaming is sovereignty negotiated.
img.title: GAMING COMPACTS

questions.question: Comparing state and tribal governments in New Mexico, the most accurate statement is:
questions.correctAnswer: Both are sovereign governments with constitutions, courts and police, but tribal authority flows from inherent sovereignty and treaties, while state authority flows from the United States Constitution's Tenth Amendment structure
distractors: Tribal governments are simply counties with cultural programs
The state may abolish tribal governments whenever it chooses
Tribal courts have jurisdiction over all crimes anywhere in New Mexico
questions.explanation: Dual sovereignty is the operating system: state law generally stops at reservation lines, tribal law governs internal affairs, and federal law overlays both - a structure students meet again in the civics course's Civ.31 standard.
questions.memoryHook: Two sovereignties, one map: authority from different sources.

img.scene: Two flags flying at the same height over a shared plaza, a courthouse and a tribal building beyond. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Two sovereignties, one map: authority from different sources.
img.title: DUAL SOVEREIGNTY

questions.question: New Mexico entered World War I in 1917 with a complication few states shared:
questions.correctAnswer: Pancho Villa's 1916 raid on Columbus, New Mexico had already put the border at war and National Guardsmen on patrol
distractors: Its governor refused to send any soldiers at all
It was still a territory awaiting statehood in 1917
Its entire population spoke only German
questions.explanation: Villa's raiders killed 18 Americans at Columbus in March 1916; Pershing's Punitive Expedition chased him into Mexico. When world war came, New Mexicans served in notable numbers, including many Spanish-speaking and Native soldiers.
questions.memoryHook: Columbus 1916: New Mexico met war before the nation did.

img.scene: A dusty border town main street with a water tower, cavalry horses at a rail, morning haze. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Columbus 1916: New Mexico met war before the nation did.
img.title: COLUMBUS, 1916

questions.question: The Rough Riders of 1898 had already tied New Mexico to national war memory because:
questions.correctAnswer: Hundreds of New Mexicans volunteered for Theodore Roosevelt's regiment in the Spanish-American War, strengthening the territory's statehood case
distractors: They were composed entirely of Apache scouts
They fought their only battle inside New Mexico
Roosevelt governed New Mexico after the war
questions.explanation: New Mexico supplied four troops of the First Volunteer Cavalry; their San Juan Hill service was Exhibit A in Washington that the territory's loyalty - and its Spanish-speaking soldiers - deserved statehood.
questions.memoryHook: Rough Riders from New Mexico argued statehood with service.

img.scene: Volunteer cavalrymen in slouch hats beside their horses at a training camp, flags behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Rough Riders from New Mexico argued statehood with service.
img.title: ROUGH RIDERS

questions.question: During the Great Depression, New Mexico's most distinctive federal relief legacy is:
questions.correctAnswer: New Deal programs - CCC camps, WPA art and building projects - that employed thousands and reshaped public buildings statewide
distractors: A state decision to refuse all federal relief money
The conversion of all farms to cotton plantations
A gold rush that ended unemployment in 1931
questions.explanation: With per-capita income among the nation's lowest, New Mexico leaned hard on the New Deal: CCC boys built trails and dams, WPA writers recorded folklore, and artists painted murals in courthouses that still hang today.
questions.memoryHook: The New Deal built New Mexico's public face.

img.scene: Young workers building a stone trail structure on a mountain slope with hand tools. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The New Deal built New Mexico's public face.
img.title: THE NEW DEAL BUILDS

questions.question: The Dust Bowl reached New Mexico's eastern plains in the 1930s, where counties like Union and Harding suffered:
questions.correctAnswer: Blowing topsoil, farm failure and out-migration as drought and plowing met on marginal grassland
distractors: Flooding that turned the plains into lakes
Volcanic ashfall from western eruptions
A plague of locusts found nowhere else
questions.explanation: Black blizzards buried fences in the northeastern plains while the southern plains states emptied. Soil conservation districts - a New Mexico contribution to the response - taught contour farming and reseeding that outlasted the decade.
questions.memoryHook: Black blizzards on the high plains taught soil conservation.

img.scene: A dust storm wall rolling toward a small plains farmstead, fences half buried in drifted soil. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Black blizzards on the high plains taught soil conservation.
img.title: DUST ON THE PLAINS

questions.question: World War II transformed Albuquerque most directly through:
questions.correctAnswer: Kirtland Field (now Kirtland Air Force Base), which trained tens of thousands of airmen and anchored a permanent military economy
distractors: A naval shipyard built on the Rio Grande
The relocation of the state capital there in 1942
Its selection as the site of the first atomic test
questions.explanation: Kirtland trained bombardiers and pilots and later hosted weapons work tied to Sandia. Wartime Albuquerque roughly doubled, beginning its shift from rail town to the state's military-scientific metropolis.
questions.memoryHook: Kirtland turned a rail town into a garrison city.

img.scene: Rows of training aircraft on a desert airfield apron with a mesa backdrop, ground crews at work. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
